A flat connection in differential geometry is a connection whose curvature is zero. Intuitively, this means that parallel transport along any path in the given space will preserve the geometric structure that the connection measures. A Euclidean space with its standard connection (where straight lines are geodesics and angles between vectors are preserved under parallel transport) is an example of a flat connection in terms of Riemannian geometry.

A projectively flat connection, on the other hand, is a connection whose projective holonomy group is trivial. Here, "projective" refers to the notion that only ratios of distances matter, not the absolute values. In other words, parallel transport along any path will only preserve angles but not necessarily the length of vectors. An example of a space with a projectively flat connection is the sphere, where parallel transport is defined by the spherical geometry.

To summarize, in a space with a flat connection, parallel transport preserves all of the geometric structure(segments and angles), while in a projectively flat space, only "directions" (i.e., the projective structure) are preserved by parallel transport. It's a more flexible concept.

This means flat connections are always projectively flat, but the converse is not true.
